gloss_terse: The foresail or mainsail of a ship, a nautical term for the principal sail used in navigation
gloss_readable: In nautical contexts, this refers to a ship's foresail or main sail, the primary canvas used to catch wind and propel the vessel forward. The term appears in Acts during Paul's dramatic shipwreck narrative, where the crew hoisted this sail to beach the ship. Ancient Mediterranean sailors depended on such sails for navigation, making this a technical maritime term that Luke preserves with precision.

senses.1: The singular occurrence in Acts 27:40 describes the crew raising the foresail as they attempted to run the ship aground on Malta's shore. The multilingual evidence (Spanish 'vela-de-proa' = prow-sail, French 'voile' = sail) confirms the nautical specificity of this rare New Testament term, preserved only in Luke's detailed shipwreck account.

gloss_terse: Newborn, just-born; describing infants in their earliest stage of life
gloss_readable: This compound word literally means 'just-generated' or 'newly-born,' emphasizing the extreme youth and fresh beginning of an infant's life. Peter uses it metaphorically in his first epistle, urging believers to crave spiritual nourishment like newborn babies instinctively desire milk. The image captures both vulnerability and intense hunger, painting Christian discipleship as a natural, life-sustaining need rather than mere duty.

senses.1: Peter's metaphor in 1 Peter 2:2 draws on the universal image of nursing infants to describe spiritual appetite. The translations consistently emphasize 'newborn' status (Spanish 'recién-nacidos,' German 'neugeboren'), highlighting the fresh, dependent state that should characterize believers' relationship to God's word, craving it as naturally as babies crave mother's milk.

gloss_terse: Complete, perfect, fully equipped; fitted exactly for its purpose or thoroughly prepared
gloss_readable: Classical Greek used this word to describe things 'complete of their kind' or 'exactly fitted'—armor that matches perfectly, words spoken to the purpose, minds in accord. Paul adopts it in 2 Timothy to describe the God-breathed Scripture's effect: making the servant of God 'complete' or 'thoroughly equipped' for every good work. It conveys not mere adequacy but comprehensive preparation, the kind of wholeness that leaves nothing lacking.

senses.1: In 2 Timothy 3:17, Paul describes Scripture's goal as producing someone who is 'complete' (Spanish 'completo,' German 'vollkommen' = perfect). The word's classical sense of being 'exactly fitted' or 'suitable' enriches the verse—God's word doesn't just inform but comprehensively equips, producing workers who are whole, mature, and ready for any task God assigns.

gloss_terse: Arphaxad, a patriarch listed in Luke's genealogy of Jesus, son of Shem and ancestor of Abraham
gloss_readable: Arphaxad (from Hebrew אַרְפַּכְשַׁד) appears in Luke's genealogy as a post-flood patriarch, son of Shem and grandfather of Eber. Genesis 11 records him being born two years after the flood and living 438 years. Luke traces Jesus' lineage through this ancient ancestor to establish Christ's connection to the promises given to Abraham's line, grounding the gospel in the oldest streams of biblical history.

senses.1: Luke 3:36 places Arphaxad in the genealogical chain between Shem and Shelah. The consistent transliteration across languages (Spanish 'Arphaxád,' French 'Arphaxad') reflects the Hebrew original. This genealogical link connects Jesus not just to Abraham but to the post-diluvian renewal of humanity, emphasizing the universal scope of God's redemptive plan through one particular family line.

gloss_terse: Archelaus, son of Herod the Great, who ruled Judea, Samaria, and Idumea after his father's death
gloss_readable: Archelaus inherited the most significant portion of his father Herod the Great's kingdom but proved so brutal and incompetent that Rome deposed him after only nine years. Matthew mentions him precisely because Joseph and Mary, returning from Egypt with the child Jesus, feared to settle in Judea under his rule and went instead to Galilee. This single reference captures a crucial moment when political brutality shaped the holy family's geography.

senses.1: In Matthew 2:22, Joseph's fear of Archelaus redirects the family to Nazareth in Galilee rather than Bethlehem in Judea. The historical Archelaus was notorious for violence, eventually banished by Rome in AD 6. This brief mention, transliterated identically across languages, explains why Jesus grew up in Nazareth rather than his birthplace—a detail that would later puzzle his opponents ('Can anything good come from Nazareth?').

gloss_terse: High-priestly, pertaining to or characteristic of the office of high priest
gloss_readable: This adjective describes anything belonging to or associated with the high priest's office and family. In Acts, Luke uses it to identify the 'high-priestly family' or those of high-priestly lineage who wielded religious and political power in Jerusalem. The term captures the aristocratic, hereditary nature of temple leadership in first-century Judaism, where genealogy and office were inseparable.

senses.1: Acts 4:6 refers to those 'of the high-priestly family' (Spanish 'sumo-sacerdotal' = supreme-priestly, French 'souverain-sacrificateur' = sovereign-priest) who gathered to question Peter and John. This describes not just the reigning high priest but the aristocratic clan from which high priests were chosen, families like Annas and Caiaphas who controlled temple affairs and collaborated with Roman power.

gloss_terse: Chief shepherd, a title emphasizing supreme pastoral authority and oversight
gloss_readable: This compound word combines 'chief' with 'shepherd,' creating a title that Peter applies to Christ as the supreme pastor over all under-shepherds. In a letter written to church elders about their pastoral duties, Peter points them to the coming revelation of the 'Chief Shepherd' who will reward faithful service. The term distinguishes Jesus from human pastors while affirming their shared shepherding role under his ultimate authority.

senses.1: In 1 Peter 5:4, after instructing elders to shepherd God's flock willingly, Peter promises that when the 'Chief Shepherd' appears, faithful pastors will receive an unfading crown. The Spanish 'Príncipe-de-pastores' (Prince of shepherds) and German 'Erzhirte' (arch-shepherd) capture the hierarchical image: human shepherds serve under the supreme Shepherd, accountable to him and rewarded by him.

gloss_terse: Master builder, chief architect; one who designs and directs construction projects
gloss_readable: Classical Greek distinguished the master builder or architect who designed and supervised construction from the laborers who carried out the work. Paul adopts this metaphor in 1 Corinthians, describing himself as a 'wise master builder' who laid the gospel foundation in Corinth, while others now build upon it. The term emphasizes both skill and responsibility—the architect's work determines whether the whole structure will stand or fall.

senses.1: In 1 Corinthians 3:10, Paul describes himself as a 'wise master builder' (Spanish 'arquitecto,' French 'architecte,' German 'Baumeister') who laid the foundation of Christ in the Corinthian church. The metaphor distinguishes his apostolic work of founding the church from others' subsequent ministry of building on that foundation. Like an architect, Paul's initial design work was crucial—he established the gospel pattern on which everything else must be constructed.

gloss_terse: Chief tax collector, a senior official overseeing multiple tax collectors in a district
gloss_readable: This New Testament coinage describes a supervisory tax collector who managed other publicans. Zacchaeus held this position in Jericho, making him both wealthy and despised—wealthy because he took a cut from multiple collection stations, despised because he led a system that extracted Rome's tribute from his own people. The term appears nowhere else in Greek literature, seemingly Luke's precise description of Zacchaeus's particular administrative role.

senses.1: Luke 19:2 introduces Zacchaeus uniquely as a 'chief tax collector' (Spanish 'jefe-de-recaudadores' = boss of collectors). His role supervising other tax collectors in the prosperous Jericho district explains both his great wealth and the crowd's horror when Jesus chose his house for dinner. The compound term emphasizes that Zacchaeus wasn't merely a collaborator but led collaboration, making Jesus' gracious pursuit of him all the more scandalous and transformative.

gloss_terse: To act impiously or ungodly; to commit sacrilege or show contempt for divine things
gloss_readable: Classical Greek used this verb for acts of impiety or sacrilege against gods and sacred things. Jude employs it to describe the actions of false teachers who have infiltrated the church. The word carries moral weight beyond mere unbelief—it implies active contempt, deliberate violation of what is sacred, behavior that flaunts disregard for God. In Jude's apocalyptic warning, these ungodly deeds will be exposed when the Lord comes with his holy ones.

senses.1: Jude 1:15 repeats 'ungodly' four times in rapid succession (ungodly sinners, ungodly deeds, acted ungodly), emphasizing the comprehensive impiety of false teachers. The Spanish 'obraron impíamente' (they worked impiously) and German 'gottlos handelten' (godlessly acted) capture the active nature of the offense—not passive unbelief but deliberate sacrilege. The threefold repetition creates a drumbeat of judgment against those who corrupt the faith from within.

gloss_terse: Insignificant, undistinguished, without distinguishing marks; ordinary or obscure
gloss_readable: Originally referring to uncoined gold or unmarked objects, this word evolved to describe people or places lacking distinction or fame. Paul uses it in Acts when arrested in Jerusalem, protesting that he is 'a citizen of no insignificant city'—a rhetorically clever way of saying Tarsus was actually quite important. The double negative highlights civic pride while maintaining diplomatic modesty before a Roman tribune.

senses.1: In Acts 21:39, Paul describes Tarsus as 'no insignificant city' (Spanish 'insignificante,' French 'sans marque' = without mark). The litotes (understatement through negation) diplomatically asserts Tarsus's importance—it was a major intellectual and commercial center, capital of Cilicia. Paul's phrasing shows rhetorical skill: he defends his standing without boasting, letting the double negative carry the weight of civic reputation.

gloss_terse: Weakness, ailment; a condition of physical frailty or moral/spiritual limitation
gloss_readable: This noun describes various forms of weakness—bodily ailments, moral limitations, or spiritual vulnerabilities. Paul uses it in Romans to discuss how mature Christians should bear with the 'weaknesses' of those with tender consciences. The term shifts depending on context between physical infirmity and moral or spiritual limitation, always implying a state that needs support or accommodation from stronger brothers and sisters.

senses.1: Romans 15:1 urges the strong to 'bear the weaknesses' (Spanish 'debilidades,' German 'Schwachheiten') of those without strength. Paul refers to scruples about food, drink, and holy days that trouble some believers' consciences. These 'weaknesses' aren't sins but limitations—areas where some Christians haven't yet grasped their freedom in Christ. The strong should accommodate these tender consciences rather than insisting on their rights.

gloss_terse: Asians, people from the Roman province of Asia (western Asia Minor)
gloss_readable: This term identifies people from the Roman province of Asia, roughly modern-day western Turkey, which included important cities like Ephesus, Smyrna, and Pergamum. In Acts, 'Asians' refers to members of Paul's traveling party who accompanied him from this region. The province of Asia was one of Rome's wealthiest and most cultured, home to significant early Christian communities addressed in Revelation's seven letters.

senses.1: Acts 20:4 lists several 'Asians' (Spanish 'asiáticos,' French 'Asiatique') who traveled with Paul, including Tychicus and Trophimus. These representatives from the province of Asia accompanied Paul as he carried the collection for Jerusalem's poor. Their presence demonstrated the geographic spread of Paul's mission and the unity of Gentile churches with the mother church, as believers from Asia Minor partnered in supporting Jewish Christians.

gloss_terse: Asiarchs, wealthy civic leaders who sponsored festivals and imperial cult activities in the province of Asia
gloss_readable: Asiarchs were elite provincial officials in Roman Asia who funded public festivals, games, and imperial cult ceremonies. These wealthy aristocrats held prestigious positions that combined civic duty with religious responsibility, particularly maintaining the emperor cult. Luke mentions them surprisingly as Paul's friends in Ephesus, showing that the apostle had supporters even among the pagan civic elite—a detail that emphasizes Christianity's penetration across social boundaries.

senses.1: Acts 19:31 describes 'some of the Asiarchs' (Spanish 'asiarcas,' French 'Asiarque') as Paul's friends who urged him not to risk the theater riot. These provincial aristocrats, despite their role promoting imperial cult, befriended Paul and protected him from mob violence. The detail reveals Paul's broad social connections and suggests that even pagan officials recognized Christianity as distinct from the guild-based idolatry that sparked the riot.

gloss_terse: Want of food, abstinence from eating; fasting whether voluntary or involuntary
gloss_readable: This term describes going without food, whether from necessity (lack of provisions) or choice (religious fasting). In Acts, Paul uses it to describe the extended period during the storm when the ship's company ate nothing—not religious fasting but desperate deprivation amid crisis. Classical usage distinguished between involuntary hunger and deliberate abstinence, though the physical state was identical.

senses.1: Acts 27:21 refers to the sailors' 'long abstinence from food' (Spanish 'falta de alimento,' French 'jeûne,' German 'Hungerzeit') during the storm. This wasn't spiritual fasting but desperate food-deprivation—either seasickness prevented eating, or the storm made meal preparation impossible. After two weeks without proper meals, Paul urged them to eat for strength, distinguishing necessary nourishment from religious abstinence.

gloss_terse: Without food, fasting; describing persons who have eaten nothing
gloss_readable: This adjective describes people who have gone without food, whether by choice or circumstance. In Acts, it characterizes the storm-tossed sailors who had eaten nothing during their maritime ordeal. The word simply states the condition—empty stomachs—without specifying whether the abstinence was voluntary discipline or forced by circumstances. Context determines whether it implies religious fasting or mere hunger.

senses.1: Acts 27:33 describes the ship's company as 'without food' (Spanish 'sin comer,' German 'ohne Nahrung') for fourteen days. Paul urged them to eat for survival's sake, not for pleasure—they needed strength to survive the shipwreck and swim to shore. The detail emphasizes the severity of their ordeal: storm conditions so dire that even basic nourishment became impossible, leaving them weakened at the very moment they needed most strength.

gloss_terse: To practice, exercise discipline or train oneself; to cultivate a skill or virtue through deliberate effort
gloss_readable: Classical Greek used this word for working raw materials into finished products or training oneself in a skill. In moral contexts, it described the deliberate cultivation of virtue through discipline and practice. Paul employs it in Acts to describe his conscientious effort to maintain a clear conscience before God and people—not passive innocence but active, disciplined cultivation of moral integrity through constant practice.

senses.1: In Acts 24:16, Paul declares 'I practice' (Spanish 'me ejercito,' French 'exercer') to always have a clear conscience. The verb implies deliberate, ongoing effort—Paul doesn't just happen to have a clear conscience but actively works to maintain it through spiritual discipline. Like an athlete training or a craftsman honing skill, Paul exercises his conscience, cultivating sensitivity to God and others through constant practice.

gloss_terse: Gladly, with pleasure; willingly and joyfully
gloss_readable: This adverb describes doing something with genuine pleasure and satisfaction, not reluctantly or under compulsion. In Acts, it characterizes how Jerusalem believers received Paul and his companions—not merely tolerated them but welcomed them gladly. The word implies emotional warmth beyond mere politeness, the kind of reception that springs from genuine affection and shared faith.

senses.1: Acts 21:17 describes how Jerusalem believers received Paul 'gladly' (Spanish 'gozosamente,' French 'avec plaisir'). After years apart and amid tensions between Jewish and Gentile Christians, this warm reception mattered deeply. The adverb signals genuine joy, not diplomatic coolness—these believers truly delighted in Paul's arrival and the unity his visit represented between branches of the early church.

gloss_terse: Unwise, foolish; lacking sound judgment or discernment
gloss_readable: This adjective describes people who lack wisdom—not necessarily unintelligent but failing to exercise sound judgment in life's crucial matters. Paul uses it in Ephesians to contrast two ways of living: walking as unwise people who squander their days, versus walking as wise people who discern God's will and redeem the time. The term implies moral and spiritual foolishness, not mere intellectual limitation.

senses.1: Ephesians 5:15 warns against walking as 'unwise' people (Spanish 'necios' = fools, German 'unweise'). The context contrasts lifestyle choices: the unwise drift through life oblivious to God's purposes, while the wise actively discern his will and make the most of every opportunity. Paul's concern isn't IQ but spiritual discernment—recognizing what matters eternally and ordering life accordingly.

gloss_terse: Asp, a venomous snake; particularly the Egyptian cobra known for its deadly bite
gloss_readable: The asp was a poisonous serpent, often identified with the Egyptian cobra, feared throughout the ancient Mediterranean for its lethal venom. Paul quotes Psalm 140 in Romans, using the image of asp venom under lips to describe the deadly, poisonous nature of human speech when turned to slander and deceit. The metaphor captures how words can inject poison into relationships and communities, killing trust and love as surely as snake venom kills bodies.

senses.1: Romans 3:13 quotes the Psalm: 'the poison of asps is under their lips' (Spanish 'de áspides,' French 'aspic'). This vivid image describes malicious speech as carrying deadly venom—words that poison, destroy, and kill. Like a cobra's concealed fangs, the tongue hides its poison until the moment of striking. The metaphor emphasizes speech's lethal potential when weaponized for harm rather than used for blessing.

gloss_terse: Implacable, irreconcilable; refusing to make peace or honor agreements
gloss_readable: Literally 'without treaty' or 'truce-less,' this word described those who refuse to make or keep peace agreements. In moral contexts, it characterized people who won't be reconciled, who maintain hostility regardless of overtures toward peace. Paul uses it in vice lists to describe end-times godlessness—people so hardened that they refuse reconciliation, preferring perpetual enmity to the vulnerability of peacemaking.

senses.1: In 2 Timothy 3:3, Paul lists 'irreconcilable' (Spanish 'implacables,' German 'unversöhnt' = unreconciled) among vices marking the last days. The word describes those who refuse peace, who won't settle disputes or honor agreements. In an age demanding unity, such people insist on division; when offered reconciliation, they choose ongoing hostility. The vice is relational hardness—preferring the safety of enmity to the risk of peace.

gloss_terse: Nearer, closer; at a shorter distance
gloss_readable: This comparative adverb means 'nearer' or 'closer,' describing reduced distance in space. Luke uses it in Acts during the shipwreck narrative, describing how the sailors tried to sail nearer to shore before anchoring for the night. The nautical context requires precision—getting closer to land offered safety from the storm but risked running aground in darkness, requiring careful judgment about proximity.

senses.1: Acts 27:13 describes the ship sailing 'close' (Spanish 'más cerca' = more near, French 'plus près') to shore along Crete's coast. The detail captures the sailors' strategy: staying near land offered shelter from wind and currents but demanded constant vigilance to avoid rocks and reefs. The comparative adverb implies movement—not just being close but getting closer, navigating the narrow margin between safety and disaster.

gloss_terse: To be homeless or unsettled; to wander without fixed residence
gloss_readable: This verb describes lacking a stable home or fixed dwelling, wandering without secure residence. Originally used of soldiers out of position or order, it evolved to mean unsettled wandering. Paul uses it in 1 Corinthians to describe the apostles' literal homelessness—constantly moving, never settling, lacking the security of property and fixed address that most people take for granted.

senses.1: In 1 Corinthians 4:11, Paul says 'we are homeless' (Spanish 'andamos sin hogar,' French 'sans demeure fixe' = without fixed dwelling). This describes the apostolic lifestyle: constant travel, no permanent residence, the vulnerability of perpetual migration. While others enjoyed home security, the apostles wandered like refugees, their mission requiring geographic instability. The verb captures both physical displacement and the existential rootlessness of itinerant ministry.

gloss_terse: Asyncritus, a Christian in Rome greeted by Paul in his epistle
gloss_readable: The name means 'incomparable' or 'without comparison,' possibly indicating this person's distinctive character or simply a common Greco-Roman name. Paul greets Asyncritus along with four others in Romans 16, suggesting a house church or close-knit group of believers in Rome. We know nothing else about him, but his inclusion in Paul's greetings indicates he was a valued member of the Roman Christian community.

senses.1: Romans 16:14 sends greetings to Asyncritus (consistently transliterated across languages) along with Phlegon, Hermes, Patrobas, and Hermas. The cluster of names suggests either a house church or a circle of friends who met together. Paul's personal greeting, despite never having visited Rome, shows the interconnected network of early Christianity—news and relationships spread through traveling believers who kept distant congregations connected.

gloss_terse: Disagreeing, in discord; not harmonious or in agreement with one another
gloss_readable: Literally 'not harmonious' or 'dissonant,' this word described sounds that clash rather than blend, or people whose views don't align. In Acts, Luke uses it to describe the Jerusalem Jewish leaders leaving Paul's hearing in disagreement among themselves about his message. The word captures discord—not violent conflict but fundamental lack of harmony, like instruments playing different tunes simultaneously.

senses.1: Acts 28:25 describes the Jewish leaders departing 'in disagreement' (Spanish 'en desacuerdo,' French 'incompatible') with each other after Paul's testimony. His gospel message divided them—some found it persuasive, others rejected it. The adjective emphasizes their mutual discord, not unified opposition but fragmented response. Luke's narrative shows how the gospel creates division even within homogeneous groups, forcing individuals to take distinct positions.

gloss_terse: Faithless, covenant-breaking; refusing to honor agreements or keep commitments
gloss_readable: Literally 'not bound by covenant,' this word described people who break agreements, violate treaties, or refuse to honor commitments they've made. In Greco-Roman culture built on patronage and reciprocal obligations, being 'without covenant' marked someone as fundamentally untrustworthy. Paul uses it in Romans to characterize pagan depravity—societies where promises mean nothing and no agreement holds.

senses.1: Romans 1:31 lists 'faithless' (Spanish 'sin pacto' = without pact, French 'sans alliance,' German 'treulos' = loyaltyless) among marks of humanity under God's wrath. The word describes covenant-breaking, promise-ignoring, treaty-violating behavior. In ancient cultures where agreements undergirded all social order, such faithlessness threatened civilization itself. Paul sees it as symptomatic of life without God—when divine covenant is rejected, all human covenants become unstable.

gloss_terse: Unpresentable, unseemly; parts of the body considered improper to display publicly
gloss_readable: This adjective described what was considered indecorous or improper to show—body parts that culture deemed private. Paul uses it metaphorically in 1 Corinthians to discuss church unity, arguing that the body's 'unpresentable parts' receive special honor through clothing, teaching that seemingly less honorable church members deserve particular respect and care from the community.

senses.1: In 1 Corinthians 12:23, Paul describes 'unpresentable parts' (Spanish 'indecorosos,' French 'inconvenant') that we treat with special modesty through clothing. The metaphor teaches how churches should value all members: those who seem less honorable deserve greater honor, just as we clothe private body parts with particular care. The argument reverses worldly values—God's design gives special dignity to what seems shameful.

gloss_terse: Recklessly, dissolutely; in a manner characterized by wasteful excess and moral abandon
gloss_readable: This adverb describes living without restraint or regard for consequences—recklessly wasting resources and abandoning moral boundaries. Jesus uses it in the prodigal son parable to characterize the younger son's lifestyle in the far country. The word captures both financial recklessness (squandering inheritance) and moral dissolution (loose living), painting a picture of life utterly unmoored from wisdom, family, and faith.

senses.1: Luke 15:13 describes the prodigal son squandering his inheritance living 'recklessly' (Spanish 'perdidamente' = ruinously, French 'en débauche' = in debauchery). The adverb captures the totality of his abandon—not careful sin but reckless plunge into excess. He didn't preserve anything for tomorrow, didn't maintain any moral boundaries. The word choice emphasizes how far he fell and how complete his wastage became before he 'came to himself.'

gloss_terse: To be disorderly or undisciplined; to live in an irregular, irresponsible manner
gloss_readable: Originally a military term for soldiers out of formation or failing their duties, this verb evolved to describe any undisciplined, disorderly living. Paul uses it in 2 Thessalonians to defend his conduct in Thessalonica, insisting he didn't live irresponsibly but worked to support himself. The word implies failing to discharge proper responsibilities, living without the discipline that community life requires.

senses.1: In 2 Thessalonians 3:7, Paul declares 'we were not disorderly' (Spanish 'fuimos desordenados,' German 'unordentlich leben' = live disorderly) while among the Thessalonians. The context involves self-support through manual labor—Paul didn't burden the church financially but worked night and day. His point: apostles modeled responsible, disciplined living rather than the idle, mooching behavior some Thessalonians had adopted while awaiting Christ's return.

gloss_terse: Disorderly, undisciplined; living irresponsibly without proper attention to duties and obligations
gloss_readable: This adjective describes people living without proper order or discipline—failing responsibilities, ignoring duties, conducting life irregularly rather than according to accepted norms. Paul uses it in 1 Thessalonians to identify certain church members who needed admonition for their undisciplined lifestyle. The military background of the term suggests people out of position, not fulfilling their assigned roles in the community.

senses.1: First Thessalonians 5:14 urges believers to 'admonish the disorderly' (Spanish 'desordenados,' German 'unordentlich'). Context suggests these were idle believers, possibly those who quit working while awaiting Christ's return. Paul distinguishes them from the fainthearted and weak, who need encouragement and support—the disorderly need correction for their irresponsible, undisciplined behavior that burdens the community and dishonors the gospel.

gloss_terse: An indivisible moment, an instant; the smallest possible unit of time
gloss_readable: Originally describing something physically indivisible (like atoms), this word came to mean the briefest possible moment—time so short it cannot be subdivided. Paul uses it in 1 Corinthians to describe the resurrection's speed: in one indivisible instant, at the last trumpet, mortality will be swallowed by immortality. The word emphasizes suddenness and totality—not gradual transformation but instantaneous, atomic change.

senses.1: First Corinthians 15:52 promises resurrection 'in an instant' (Spanish 'instante,' French 'atome,' German 'Augenblick' = blink of eye), 'in the twinkling of an eye.' The doubled time expressions emphasize absolute brevity—change happening so fast it defies measurement. The Greek philosophical term for indivisible particles becomes a vivid image for the instantaneous transformation awaiting believers when Christ returns and death is conquered completely.

gloss_terse: Attalia, a seaport city in Pamphylia on the southern coast of Asia Minor
gloss_readable: Named after its founder Attalus II of Pergamum, Attalia served as Pamphylia's main seaport on the Mediterranean coast. Luke mentions it as Paul and Barnabas's departure point after their first missionary journey—they preached in nearby Perga, then traveled to Attalia to catch a ship back to Syrian Antioch. The city's harbor made it a natural gateway for travel between inland Asia Minor and the wider Mediterranean world.

senses.1: Acts 14:25 records Paul and Barnabas going down to Attalia to sail home after establishing churches in Galatia. The modern Turkish city Antalya preserves the ancient name. The mention shows Luke's geographic precision and highlights how the early Christian mission depended on Roman infrastructure—roads to reach inland cities, harbors like Attalia for maritime connections that enabled the gospel's rapid spread across the empire.

gloss_terse: To shine forth or illuminate; to give light or make visible through radiance
gloss_readable: This verb describes light shining forth, illuminating what was dark or making visible what was hidden. Paul uses it in 2 Corinthians regarding the gospel's light—Satan blinds unbelievers' minds to prevent the light of Christ's gospel from shining on them. The word implies both revelation (making visible) and transformation (illumination that changes what it touches).

senses.1: Second Corinthians 4:4 speaks of preventing the gospel's light 'from shining' (Spanish 'iluminar,' French 'briller,' German 'erleuchten' = enlighten). Satan blinds minds specifically to block this illumination—the light of knowing Christ's glory. The metaphor portrays spiritual blindness as blocked light: the glory is present, radiating, but veiled minds can't receive it. Conversion is the unveiling, allowing divine light to shine in and transform the inner person.

gloss_terse: Dawn, daybreak; the first light of morning as the sun rises
gloss_readable: This noun describes the dawn—that liminal moment when night yields to day, darkness to light. Homer used it for sunlight and rays; later writers employed it specifically for the breaking of dawn. Luke uses it in Acts to mark the temporal setting of Paul's extended teaching in Troas—he spoke until daybreak, the moment when Eutychus fell from the window. Dawn marks transition, the boundary between night's dangers and day's clarity.

senses.1: Acts 20:11 records Paul talking until 'dawn' (Spanish 'alba,' French 'aube,' German 'Morgendämmerung') after breaking bread in Troas. The all-night session culminated at daybreak—Paul taught from evening through midnight (when Eutychus fell), continuing until sunrise. The detail emphasizes his urgency to impart everything possible before departure, and the believers' hunger to receive teaching, willing to sacrifice sleep for apostolic instruction.

gloss_terse: Augustus, the title adopted by Octavian as Rome's first emperor; also used as an adjective meaning 'august' or 'revered'
gloss_readable: Augustus (Latin for 'revered' or 'worthy of worship') was the title Octavian took when he became Rome's first emperor in 27 BC, ending the Republic and beginning the Principate. Luke dates Jesus' birth to a census decreed by 'Caesar Augustus,' grounding the incarnation in verifiable history. The title carried religious overtones—augustus implied divinity, making Luke's use theologically loaded: the eternal Son entered time during the reign of a man claiming divine honors.

senses.1: Luke 2:1 dates Jesus' birth to a decree from 'Caesar Augustus' (consistently transliterated across languages). The historical precision anchors the incarnation in the reign of Rome's first emperor (27 BC – AD 14). The irony is profound: Augustus, celebrated as divine savior who brought peace to the empire, unknowingly set in motion (through his census) the arrival of the true Prince of Peace in an obscure Judean village.

gloss_terse: To exercise authority over, dominate; to control or govern another person
gloss_readable: This verb means to wield authority or exercise dominion over someone. In classical usage it could describe legitimate authority but sometimes implied autocratic domination. Paul uses it in 1 Timothy regarding women's role in church teaching, prohibiting them from 'exercising authority over' men in the congregational setting. The word's precise nuance is debated—whether it means normal authority or something more like domineering—affecting how interpreters understand Paul's instruction.

senses.1: First Timothy 2:12 forbids women 'to exercise authority' (Spanish 'ejercer autoridad,' German 'Gewalt ausüben' = wield power) over men in teaching contexts. The verb's background includes both legitimate authority and autocratic domination, making interpretation complex. Paul prohibits women from the authoritative teaching role in gathered worship, though the exact scope (all teaching? only congregational? only over men?) and rationale continue to generate discussion among interpreters.

gloss_terse: Flute, pipe; a wind instrument played by blowing across holes to produce musical tones
gloss_readable: The aulos was a reed instrument similar to a modern oboe or clarinet, central to Greek music for celebrations, worship, and mourning. Paul uses it in 1 Corinthians to argue that even musical instruments need distinct tones to convey meaning—if flute or harp plays unclear notes, how will anyone know the tune? The analogy teaches that spiritual gifts, especially tongues, must communicate intelligibly or they fail their purpose.

senses.1: First Corinthians 14:7 mentions 'a flute' (Spanish 'flauta,' French 'flûte,' German 'Flöte') alongside the harp to illustrate the necessity of distinction in tones. If the instrument makes no clear melody, no one can dance or sing along. Paul applies this to tongues: speech without interpretation is noise, not communication. Even non-rational instruments must produce distinct sounds; how much more should rational humans speak clearly when building up the church.

gloss_terse: Self-sufficient, content; having enough in oneself without needing external resources
gloss_readable: Classical philosophy celebrated autarkeia as the sage's ideal—needing nothing beyond oneself, independent of external circumstances. Paul adopts this Stoic term but redefines it: his sufficiency comes not from inner resources but from Christ who strengthens him. He has 'learned the secret of being content' in all circumstances—not self-powered independence but Christ-sustained contentment that transcends material conditions.

senses.1: Philippians 4:11 shows Paul claiming to be 'self-sufficient' or 'content' in all circumstances. The Greek philosophical ideal gets radically redefined—Paul's contentment isn't Stoic self-reliance but dependence on Christ: 'I can do all things through him who strengthens me.' True autarkeia is Christ-sufficiency, finding abundance or scarcity equally acceptable because Christ himself is the constant resource that makes all circumstances endurable.

gloss_terse: Self-condemned; judged guilty by one's own actions or testimony
gloss_readable: This compound word describes someone condemned by their own behavior or words—they need no external judge because their actions testify against them. Paul uses it in Titus to describe divisive people who, after two warnings, stand self-condemned. Their persistence in division despite admonition reveals their true character; they condemn themselves by their refusal to repent when corrected.

senses.1: Titus 3:11 declares that a factious person, after two warnings, is 'self-condemned' (consistently transliterated or translated across languages). The repeated admonition provides opportunity to repent; refusal reveals settled choice. No further judgment is needed—the person's persistence in division after clear warning condemns them by their own actions. Their behavior, not others' judgment, exposes their character and justifies exclusion from fellowship.

gloss_terse: Eyewitnesses; those who have personally seen and observed events firsthand
gloss_readable: This noun describes people who witnessed events with their own eyes, not receiving secondhand reports. Luke uses it in his gospel prologue to distinguish authoritative sources for his narrative—he consulted eyewitnesses and servants of the word who saw Jesus' ministry directly. The term emphasizes the historical foundation of Christian faith: not myth or speculation but testimony from people who were there, who saw and handled the Word of life.

senses.1: Luke 1:2 references those who 'from the beginning were eyewitnesses' (Spanish 'testigos oculares,' French 'témoin oculaire,' German 'Augenzeugen') and servants of the word. Luke grounds his gospel in reliable testimony from people who personally witnessed Jesus' life, death, and resurrection. This distinguishes Christianity from mystery religions—it claims historical events, verifiable through witnesses who staked their lives on what they'd seen with their own eyes.
